## Today

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Core idea
Data are not neutral facts. Data are constructed evidence.
:::

Today we discuss:

1. data provenance
2. units, populations, and variables
3. dark data
4. survey and public-sector data issues
5. data quality as part of the research answer

## The innocent spreadsheet

A data file can look clean:

| district | flooded | income | drainage | weight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Paramaribo | 1 | 2 | 0 | 1.42 |
| Wanica | 0 | 3 | 1 | 0.86 |
| Nickerie | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1.12 |

But each column hides a story:

- who collected this?
- what counted as "flooded"?
- who was not reached?
- why is there a weight?
- what is the population behind these rows?

::: {.callout-warning}
# The trap
A clean data file is not the same as clean evidence.
:::

## Data provenance

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
# Data provenance
The history of how data came into existence, moved through systems, and became available for analysis.
:::

Good provenance questions:

- Who collected the data?
- For what purpose?
- Under what procedures?
- With what definitions?
- For whom or what are the data representative?

::: footer
See Groves et al. (2009). *Survey Methodology*. Wiley; also see UNICEF MICS documentation and World Bank Microdata Library for examples of survey documentation.
:::

## Example: MICS Suriname 2018

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="55%"}
The Suriname 2018 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey was designed to provide high quality data on children, adolescents, women, and households; monitor national goals and SDG indicators; and produce disaggregated data to identify disparities.

This is a powerful dataset. It is also a dataset with a purpose.
:::

:::{.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
# Ask
If MICS was designed to monitor children, women, households, and SDGs, what questions is it naturally good for?

What questions might it not be good for?
:::
:::
::::

::: footer
UNICEF MICS Suriname 2018 Survey Findings Report and World Bank Microdata Library: [Suriname MICS 2018](https://microdata.worldbank.org/index.php/catalog/3531).
:::

## Unit of observation vs unit of analysis

These are often confused.

| Concept | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of observation | What one row describes | child, household, person, plot, district-year |
| Unit of analysis | What your question is about | child learning, household risk, district trend |

::: {.callout-important}
# Be careful
You can have child-level data, household-level predictors, and district-level weather in one project.

That does not make all units interchangeable.
:::

## Population, sample, and target

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Target population
The group you want your answer to speak about.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
# Observed sample
The cases that made it into your data.
:::
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
A mismatch creates uncertainty:

- not everyone was sampled
- not everyone responded
- some groups were not covered
- some cases were removed
- some data cannot be accessed
:::
::::

::: {.callout-warning}
# Question
Are you analyzing the population you care about, or the population the data happened to capture?
:::

## Variables are measurements

A variable is not a concept.

| Concept | Possible measurement | Possible problem |
|---|---|---|
| Poverty | income, assets, deprivation index | underreporting, informal economy |
| Trust | survey question | translation, scale interpretation |
| Flood exposure | self-report, map overlay, sensor | recall bias, spatial mismatch |
| Health | diagnosis, symptoms, biomarker | access to care, measurement error |

::: {.callout-tip}
# In short
A column name is a promise. Measurement tells you whether the promise was kept.
:::

## Administrative categories are not nature

Public-sector data are often created to run systems:

- tax collection
- social assistance
- school registration
- health administration
- permits and licenses
- disaster reports

These categories are useful. They are not always scientific constructs.

::: {.callout-warning}
# Hmmm...
When does an administrative category become a bad proxy for the thing you actually want to study?
:::

## Dark data

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
# Dark data
Information that is not available, but necessary to arrive at the correct answer.
:::

Dark data can be:

- missing values
- nonresponse
- undercoverage
- hidden populations
- unmeasured confounders
- changed definitions over time
- data that exist, but cannot be accessed

## A small taxonomy of darkness

| Dark data problem | Example | Possible consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Missing values | income not reported | biased inequality estimates |
| Nonresponse | remote households not reached | undercoverage of vulnerable groups |
| Unmeasured confounding | drainage quality not measured | misleading flood-risk explanation |
| Hidden populations | informal workers absent from registers | official picture too optimistic |
| Changed definitions | fiscal categories revised | trend break mistaken for real change |
| Restricted access | detailed location unavailable | spatial analysis becomes weaker |

## Example: flood risk in Paramaribo

The World Bank's strategic flood risk assessment for Paramaribo emphasizes coastal, fluvial, and pluvial flood risk, drainage, land use, and climate-related challenges.

A household survey about wateroverlast may observe **reported water nuisance**.

It may not observe:

- exact water depth
- blocked drainage at the time of rainfall
- illegal dumping
- elevation at household level
- previous mitigation actions
- households that moved away after repeated floods

::: footer
World Bank. *Paramaribo Strategic Flood Risk Assessment: Final Report*. [PDF](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/463821538552629012/pdf/Suriname-FRA-REPORT-FINAL.pdf).
:::

## The painful question

::: {.callout-important}
# What would change your answer?
If a missing variable could change your conclusion, it belongs in your limitations.
:::

For a flood-risk project:

- rainfall may be measured at district level
- flooding may be reported by households
- drainage may be observed crudely
- wealth may be a proxy for housing quality

The answer can still be useful.

But it must be honest about what it does not see.

## Survey data: design is part of the data

Survey data are not just rows.

They often include:

- strata
- clusters
- sampling weights
- household selection procedures
- response rates
- eligibility rules
- questionnaire routing

::: {.callout-tip}
# Good practice
Read the methodology section before touching the analysis file.
:::

::: footer
UNICEF MICS programme documentation and survey reports include questionnaires, sampling design information, and weights. See [MICS surveys](https://mics.unicef.org/surveys).
:::

## Why weights exist

Weights often correct for:

- unequal selection probabilities
- nonresponse adjustments
- calibration to known population totals

A weighted answer and an unweighted answer can differ.

::: {.callout-warning}
# Be careful
If a survey was designed with weights, ignoring them may change the population your answer speaks about.
:::

## Clustering and stratification

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note}
# Clustering
People in the same cluster may be more similar than people in different clusters.
:::

Examples:

- households in the same enumeration area
- students in the same school
- workers in the same organization
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note}
# Stratification
Sampling may be organized to guarantee representation across subgroups.
:::

Examples:

- district
- urban/rural area
- region
- demographic groups
:::
::::

Ignoring design can make uncertainty look smaller than it is.

## Public-sector data: collected for action

Administrative data can be extremely valuable.

But the data generating process may change when policy changes:

- eligibility rules change
- reporting systems change
- incentives change
- definitions change
- enforcement changes
- digital systems replace paper systems

::: {.callout-important}
# Trend warning
A trend in the data can be a trend in the world, or a trend in the measurement system.
:::

## Example: public opinion data

LAPOP's AmericasBarometer is a regional public-opinion survey project with nationally representative samples of voting-age adults across countries in the Americas.

This is valuable for questions about public trust, corruption perceptions, and democratic attitudes.

But a survey response is still a measurement:

- question wording matters
- timing matters
- response scales matter
- social desirability matters
- nonresponse matters

::: footer
LAPOP Lab / Vanderbilt University, [AmericasBarometer](https://www.vanderbilt.edu/lapop/about-americasbarometer.php); Roper Center summary of LAPOP methodology: [Latin American Public Opinion Project](https://ropercenter.cornell.edu/latin-american-public-opinion-project-lapop).
:::

## Codebooks are not optional

A codebook tells you:

- variable meanings
- value labels
- missing value codes
- skip patterns
- questionnaire wording
- units and scales
- eligibility restrictions

::: {.callout-warning}
# Classic mistake
Treating `99`, `999`, `-8`, or `Don't know` as real numbers.
:::

## Data quality is not a paragraph at the end

Data quality shapes:

- the research question
- the analysis plan
- the strength of the claim
- the interpretation
- the limitations
- the recommendation

::: {.callout-tip}
# In short
Your result is only as credible as the data-generating process allows.
:::

## Claim language

Weak data do not always mean useless data.

But they do require honest language.

| Instead of | Try |
|---|---|
| X causes Y | X is associated with Y |
| The population is | In the observed sample... |
| This proves | This suggests... |
| The data show no problem | The available data do not show... |
| We controlled for everything | We accounted for observed background variables |

## To conclude

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
# Your data are witnesses
They can tell you what they saw.

They cannot tell you what they were never able to observe.
:::

Before you model, ask:

1. Where did the data come from?
2. What do the variables really measure?
3. Who or what is missing?
4. What design choices shaped the file?
5. What can this dataset answer well?
6. What can it not answer?

::: {.callout-note}
# The goal
Make the dataset visible as an argument, not just as a file.
:::
